title: Automating new-lead intake without losing the relationship
metaTitle: Lead intake that keeps a person on the reply
excerpt: File each new lead and draft the reply, then have a person send it. Automate the sorting, not the decision about fit, price, or the first real conversation.
alt: A person in a blue shirt signing a paper document with a pen. The signature is the part of lead intake a person still has to own.
caption: The signature stays with a person. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should an automated lead intake send on its own?
faqs.answer: A receipt that only confirms the form arrived, and only if that sentence is true. The reply that accepts, declines, or asks for the next conversation should be sent by a person who checked the draft. A workflow that sends the judgment itself is no longer a handoff.

faqs.question: Which form fields are worth requiring?
faqs.answer: Ask for a name, an email, and what they want, in their words. A link and a timing note can be optional, including a way to say they are not sure. Leave a required budget off the form, because people invent numbers and a later sort will treat those numbers as real.

faqs.question: How do you know the intake automation is worth keeping?
faqs.answer: Time the old sorting and the new review on real leads, and keep the workflow only if review is faster and misunderstandings do not rise. Watch the first twenty for confident mistakes, such as a wrong decline. If review takes longer than writing the reply, narrow the draft or remove it.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
AI automation lead intake should file a new enquiry and draft the first reply, then stop. A person reads the draft and sends it. The form can arrive during a build review or while the studio is closed. The relationship starts when someone who can keep a promise answers in their own name.

Treat the automation as the handoff around that form. The machine may store the lead, mark what is missing, and prepare a reply from a template you wrote. Keep a person on anything the lead will see, anything that talks about money, and anything you cannot undo. After the first real enquiries have passed through, compare the minutes you used to spend sorting with the minutes a review still takes.

## Name the handoff before you pick a tool

A lead arrives as a row. There is a name, an email, a few sentences, and sometimes a link. The old chore is the sorting. Someone opens the inbox, decides which kind of work it is, checks whether this person has written before, and writes a first note that does not start from a blank page. That sorting is what you automate. The judgment inside the note stays with a person.

Write the handoff in one sentence before you choose software. "When the contact form submits, create a record, mark the gaps, and leave a draft reply for the person on intake." If the sentence includes "and the system decides whether we want the work," you have left a handoff and built a decision the lead cannot appeal.

Hanabi builds small automations when the result is something a person already produced by hand. A draft in a queue is that shape. A tool that claims to qualify the whole pipeline is a slogan until you can point at the fields it reads and the sentences it may prepare. The output here is a record plus a draft. It is not a sent email, a calendar hold, or a price.

## What the form has to carry

The draft is only as good as the form. Ask for the facts a person needs on the first read, and ask for little else.

- Name and email, so the reply has a person to reach.
- What they want built or fixed, in their words, in a box large enough for a real sentence.
- A link to the current site or product, if one exists, marked optional so a new company is not stuck.
- Timing they already know, including a choice for "not sure."
- How they would like to be answered, if you truly offer more than one way.

Leave budget as a range someone can skip, or leave it off the form. A required budget field makes careful people invent a number. A later step that treats the invented number as a score will set aside the wrong enquiries. You can talk about money on a call, once you know what the work is.

Do not ask for a paragraph you will not read. Every extra box is a reason to abandon the form, and it gives the draft more text to misunderstand. If you need a file, ask after a person has replied, when you know which file matters. Write the labels as questions. "Tell us what you need" can be answered. A slogan in the label cannot, and the draft will have nothing solid to quote.

## Four jobs for the machine

On submit, the workflow can do four jobs. More than four is how a simple handoff becomes a system nobody wants to open.

1. Store the lead where the intake person already looks, with the time it arrived.
2. Flag a likely duplicate against email, so two tabs do not become two relationships and two replies.
3. Mark missing facts in plain language, such as "no link" or "timing left blank."
4. Draft a reply from a template the studio wrote, filled only with facts that appear on the form.

The draft has three shapes. A person chooses the shape with rules you can say out loud. One shape asks for the single missing fact. One shape offers a way to talk because the request matches work you do. One shape declines, briefly, because the request sits outside that work. The decline is the shape to guard. A wrong no is hard to walk back, and the lead will see it.

A template, not a client story: the form says the sender wants a marketing site for a product that already has users, and it includes a link. The draft may name that site and offer a time to talk about scope. It may not claim you have reviewed the product or know the cost. Those sentences were not on the form.

Name the person who owns intake this week. "The team" is not a name. If that person is away, the workflow tells a second person and still does not send the draft. Sending mail to cover a gap is how an unreviewed reply leaves.

## The reply a person still sends

The lead will see the email. That alone puts it on the list of things a person keeps. People read under time pressure. Nielsen Norman Group's write-up of page-visit research, [How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/), is the useful picture. Users often leave a web page in 10 to 20 seconds. The average visit lasts a little less than a minute, and people have time to read only about a quarter of the text on pages they do open. A clear value in the first 10 seconds is what earns a longer look. A first reply is a short page sitting in an inbox. The first two lines have to say who you are, that you read the request, and what happens next.

A usable reply is four lines.

- You received the note, and you name the work they described, using their words where you can.
- One specific question, or one clear next step. One, not a list of homework.
- Who will do that step, with a name.
- No price, no start date, and no promise that the work is a fit until a person has decided that it is.

Send the substantive reply from a person. A line that says the receipt was automatic is fine when the note only confirms that the form arrived. It is a poor fit on the message that accepts or declines. If you send a receipt, keep it from answering the question. Two messages that disagree are worse than a short wait.

Check the name, check that the ask matches the form, and check that a blank field did not become a guess. Then send the draft, or fix the template so the next one does not need the same repair.

[Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) cover the sites, the product interfaces, and the small automations around them. The useful version of this workflow is one checkable handoff, scoped as a piece of work.

## Decisions you do not hand over

Do not let the workflow send a proposal, a price, or a contract. Those sit next to payment, and they are awkward to undo. Do not let it place a meeting on a founder's calendar because a model was confident. A sentence that offers a way to request a time is enough inside a reply a person sends. A hold that appears on its own is a different product, and it spends the one resource a small team cannot reprint.

Do not let the draft add a warmer paragraph by guessing the lead's business. Templates are plain on purpose. The moment a draft "adds a personal touch" that was not on the form, you owe a full read anyway, and you have added a new way to be wrong. Quoting a short phrase they wrote is personal enough.

Do not score leads with a number you cannot explain on a call. If you need a sort, use rules you can read aloud: asked for a site and a brand, asked for something you do not do, or already a client. A score of 81 is not a rule. If a tool offers one, hide it until you have written the rules yourself.

The [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) from the W3C groups quality under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A reply someone must act on should make the action and the result plain. A summary that hides whether you are saying yes, no, or "one more fact" fails that test. Whether the project is a fit, and whether the timing they named is real, stays a conversation. A draft can prepare the opening. It cannot hold the opinion.

## Minutes saved against minutes of review

Before you turn the workflow on, time the old chore for five real leads. Include the search through the inbox, the check for a duplicate, and the rewriting of the same opening line. Write the number down. A guess will flatter the tool.

Then time the review on the new path. Open the draft, check the name, check that the ask matches the form, check that you are not promising work you will not do, and send or fix. If review takes longer than the old reply, remove the automation or narrow it until the draft is almost always right. A longer review means you automated a chore that was not shaped enough to hand over.

Keep two other counts for a month. One is the time from submit to the human reply, during hours you have said you answer. A draft is not a reason to answer tomorrow. The other is how often a lead writes back that you misunderstood them. If that rises, fix the template or write the reply yourself. The minutes were not the point.

## The first twenty, then a lighter check

Keep a person on the first twenty leads even when the timer looks good. The failures that matter are the confident ones. The wrong name. The decline that should have been a question. The draft that mentions a service the lead did not ask for. The duplicate that received two different replies an hour apart. After those twenty, a lighter check is reasonable on a pure receipt, if you even send one. The drafts that accept, decline, or ask for the next conversation stay with a person.

Stop if the form is too thin to draft from, and fix the form first. Stop if two people might send the same draft. One owner. Stop if the tool wants the whole inbox in order to file one form. Give it the submission, not every thread you have had with a customer. Keep the three templates and the rules that choose them where intake already works. A workflow nobody can explain on Monday is a new chore.

The next message that can strain the same relationship is the one about money owed. [Automating invoice reminders without losing the relationship](/blog/automating-invoice-reminders-without-losing-the-relationship) picks up there, when the handoff is no longer a new lead but a bill the client already expects to see.
